headline: High-risk shared filesystem and broad egress create prompt-injection, leakage, and cascading-error exposure; compliance risk is moderate.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: Both agents can read and write filesystems, so one agent’s outputs can be placed where the other may ingest them as trusted content. Replit Agent’s workspace persistence and transformers’ file-based inputs make a shared-file bridge plausible, though not proven to be automatic. This is more than manual copy-paste, but not clearly a default hijack path.
conditions: IF both agents are pointed at the same workspace directory
IF agent_b consumes files produced by agent_a without provenance checks
mitigations: Separate workspaces per agent
Add provenance labels to all handoff files
Require manual review before agent_b reads agent_a outputs
Use read-only mounts for agent_b where possible

B_data_leakage.rationale: Agent A touches secrets and deployment configuration, and both agents have broad network egress plus filesystem access. If they share a workspace, agent_b can read sensitive files and potentially transmit them via its own APIs or outputs. The pair does not prove automatic exfiltration, but the default blast radius includes secrets and source code.
conditions: IF agent_a stores secrets or deployment config in the shared workspace
IF agent_b is allowed to read those files and send derived content to external services
mitigations: Keep secrets outside shared directories
Rotate any exposed API keys
Disable network egress for agent_b during sensitive tasks
Use per-agent access controls on workspace files

C_capability_conflict.rationale: Both agents can write filesystems, execute shells, install packages, and use broad network egress. Agent A also modifies git state, so concurrent edits in a shared Repl or repo can overwrite each other or corrupt dependency state. The overlap is strong enough that default multi-instance use can cause destructive conflicts.
conditions: IF both agents operate in the same repository or Repl filesystem
IF either agent modifies git state or package dependencies while the other is active
mitigations: Run only one writer at a time
Use separate branches per agent
Freeze dependency installs during parallel work
Add file-locking or merge gates
requires-engineering: introduce orchestrator-level concurrency locks

D_cascading_error.rationale: Agent A can generate code and configuration that agent B may treat as input, and agent B can then act on it with shell, filesystem, and network tools. Without an explicit verification step, errors or hallucinations from A can cascade into B’s outputs or actions. The pair is not inherently self-correcting, so the risk is default-medium rather than low.
conditions: IF agent_b consumes agent_a-produced files or instructions as authoritative
IF no human or automated verification step is inserted between them
mitigations: Require a review checkpoint between agents
Have agent_b validate all claims against source files
Limit agent_a to draft-only outputs
Log and diff all handoffs before execution

E_compliance.rationale: Agent A explicitly handles secrets and deployment configuration, while agent B processes multimodal files and has broad egress. If regulated or sensitive data is placed into the shared workspace, differing retention or residency expectations can be violated by the pair’s default file and network behavior. The profiles do not show a specific certification mismatch, so medium is the highest supportable level.
conditions: IF regulated data is stored in the shared workspace
IF retention or residency rules require tighter controls than the pair provides
mitigations: Keep regulated data out of shared folders
Document a data-handling policy for both agents
Restrict network access during compliance-sensitive tasks
Purge temporary files after each run
